analysis.one_liner: Repeals the disclosure rules and the corporate/union funding ban for campaign-season political ads.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 55 Republican sponsors and cosponsors but never received a hearing or a vote, dying in the House Administration Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe out three key parts of the 2002 McCain-Feingold campaign finance law (the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act). Corporations and labor unions could again spend money straight from their treasuries on broadcast ads that name a candidate just before an election. Groups paying for those ads would no longer have to tell the Federal Election Commission what they spent or who they are. And ads run in coordination with a candidate's campaign would no longer count as campaign contributions subject to limits [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations and labor unions would regain the right to fund 'electioneering communications' — TV and radio ads that mention a candidate near an election — out of their general treasury funds, and the groups running them could keep their spending and identities hidden from the FEC and from voters [S2] [S3]. Broadcast ad sellers would also gain a larger market for political ads.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Corporations and unions funding political ads

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the requirement that anyone spending on electioneering communications file reports with the FEC, ending mandatory disclosure of who paid for pre-election candidate ads, with the change applied retroactively to November 6, 2002 [S3].

It lifts the ban on corporations and labor organizations making disbursements for electioneering communications, letting both use treasury money — not restricted political funds — for such ads [S2] [S3].
It removes the treatment of coordinated communications as contributions, so ads run with a candidate's campaign would no longer count as donations subject to contribution limits [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Voters would lose the disclosure record showing which corporations and unions paid for ads attacking or promoting candidates right before elections, and candidates would face a flood of anonymous money coordinated with campaigns without it counting against contribution limits. The bill frames the changes as restoring First Amendment speech rights that the 2002 law restricted [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Voters seeking to know who funds ads

drawbacks.text: Removing the FEC reporting requirement means voters could no longer find out which companies or unions paid for ads naming candidates in the final weeks of a campaign [S3].

Lifting the corporate and union prohibition re-opens the loophole the 2002 law closed, in which interest groups used unlimited general treasury money for ads that a court or campaign would treat as advocacy, while coordinated ads would no longer count as contributions at all [S2] [S3].

The retroactive effective date (back to November 6, 2002, the day before the 2002 election's 'electioneering communication' window opened) would apply the repeal as if it had been part of the original 2002 law, erasing the reporting baseline for activity that already happened [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's sponsors frame the changes as restoring First Amendment speech rights that the 2002 law restricted [S3]. The cost of that argument falls on transparency: no disclosure of who funded the ads, no ban on corporate or union treasury money, and no contribution limit on coordinated ads [S2] [S3]. For a reader deciding who is served, the trade runs mostly one way — organized money in elections gains, the public's ability to trace it is removed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Administration Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it never reached the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Roscoe Bartlett (R-MD) introduced the bill on February 9, 2005, and 54 other House Republicans signed on as original cosponsors [S4].
The same day, it was referred to the Committee on House Administration, the committee with jurisdiction over campaign finance law in the House [S5].
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — appears in the bill's action history for the remainder of the 109th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Supporters of the 2002 campaign finance rules are better off: the ban on corporate and union treasury money in election ads and the disclosure requirement stayed on the books. Members who cosponsored it also avoided ever having to take a recorded vote on repealing them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Supporters of the 2002 campaign finance rules

for.name: Rep. Roscoe Bartlett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the First Amendment Restoration Act to repeal the disclosure, funding-ban, and coordination provisions of the 2002 campaign finance law.

for.name: 54 House Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; every cosponsor was a Republican.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee of referral for campaign finance legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 55 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans; the record shows no Democratic support and no action beyond the committee referral [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would let companies fund ads naming candidates near elections straight from treasury funds, with no FEC reporting of who paid. The gain to the corporation is the loss of the public's ability to trace the money.

Unions are banned from electioneering communications under the same provision, so they would regain the identical spending right. Their spending often advocates positions their members support, but the removal of disclosure applies to them equally.
Fewer limits and no disclosure filings would likely mean more pre-election political ad buys and higher ad revenue. They have no direct stake in the transparency rules themselves.
